In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification of phospho-Ser-Thr-binding domains in proteins, the elucidation of their target motifs, and the understanding of the functional consequences of the interactions of these domains with their targets.
the identification of novel phospho-Serine/Thr-binding domains and the elucidation of the molecular basis of their interactions with phospho-Serines and/or phospho-Thr on their targets.
the identification and characterisation of novel cell cycle and DNA repair genes and the elucidation of their molecular mechanisms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
phospho-Ser/thr-binding domains are a key component of a sophisticated regulatory network that controls cell cycle and DNA repair.
the phospho-Ser/thr-binding domains are a major player in the regulation of the cell cycle and the DNA damage response.
phospho-Ser/thr-binding domains are key regulators of the cell cycle and the DNA damage response.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
phospho-Ser/thr-binding domains are key players in the cell cycle and in DNA damage signalling.
phospho-Ser/thr-binding domains have emerged to play a central role in the cell cycle and in DNA damage response, and are likely to be important targets for future drug design.
these phospho-binding domains are important regulators of cell cycle and DNA repair, but that the mechanisms by which they achieve these functions are complex and not always fully understood.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cell cycle and the DNA damage response are highly interconnected, and this connection is mediated in part through phospho-Ser and phospho-Thr binding domains.
the cell cycle is regulated by the coordinated activity of multiple phospho-Ser-Thr-binding domains that act on different targets.
these domains are not merely passive sensors of phosphorylation, but are active players in the cell cycle and the DNA damage response.
